chapter_title: A Catechumen asked the Apostle: When I would give an Offering to the Saints, shall I inflict a Wound on the Alms?
chapter_note: This kephalaion is dominated by an institutional problem (catechumen alms for the elect) presented in Q&A form (frame + pastoral). The most plausibly older substrate-like material is the long impersonal legal/medical analogy (retaliation before a judge versus a doctor cutting a wound to heal). The explicit application to catechumens/elect/church and exhortation language is later pastoral usage of the analogy.

paragraphs.temporal_note: Dialogue/Q&A frame markers (“Once again… catechumen… questioned the apostle”) with institutional roles (catechumen/elect) and first-person anxiety about alms-work; this reads as the compiling community’s question-setting rather than impersonal cosmological exposition.
Continuation of the catechumen’s question in direct address; still part of the Q&A apparatus rather than a stand-alone cosmological/correspondential teaching sequence.

Answer is direct exhortation (“Do not be frightened…”) about sin and alms, aimed at catechumen practice; even though it mentions ‘living soul’, the whole paragraph functions as pastoral reassurance/application in institutional context.

paragraphs.core_text: For this matter is like to two people, if a personal enemy and an opponent of theirs will hit one first and make a sore and a wound on his body. Afterwards he smites him again and [...] and he hits over his blows and [...] blows that have made sores on him and [...] ⟨p.237⟩ strikes him these two times [...] accuses his enemy who has struck him. And this judge questions him to his face about the [...] of the sores that he has left as marks on his body. And they [...] on him as if he had split his head. And he is led to judgement and sentence, and is punished before the judge of the world. He makes retribution for a sore in the sore place, and adds to him the wound that he had left on this person who had not yet sinned against him. He shall not omit the retaliation of the opponent, as he is judged [...] according to enmity.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Impersonal, illustrative analogical teaching (legal retaliation/judgement) without catechumen/elect/church identifiers or second-person exhortation. Not a Gospel citation; reads like a pre-institutional didactic unit used as a base for later application. (Dating remains somewhat uncertain because it is not a systematic cosmic-degree map.)

paragraphs.core_text: After the end, this enemy is condemned for the retaliation [...] sin against him. Afterwards, the other one is sick [...] the one whom this enemy has struck, and a wound comes out on him [...] and he becomes a sick person by cause of his illness, and he [...] He calls the doctor and shows him his wound. However, that doctor has no [...] nor [...] and he takes the knife to him and cuts this wound. Nevertheless, when he cuts it the blood shall pour out of his wound. That person shall be pained, but he accepts those and these things. This doctor has not retaliated nor was harm imposed on him; because he did this thing to him for healing his wound. All that he did to him was done for the good; and not directly for evil.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Continuation of the same self-contained analogy (doctor/knife/healing) explaining ‘harm for healing’ as a structural principle, still not anchored to institutional practice; likely an older teaching kernel later applied to alms-preparation.

paragraphs.core_text: After the completion, he cuts this wound and lets blood from it and heals it. He shall even make [...] gifts and compliments. That illness and the healing become a pride for this doctor, and he is given honour.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Completes the medical analogy in an impersonal narrative-teaching voice; no institutional vocabulary or audience address.

Explicit application pivot (“When you make an alms-offering you are like…”) plus institutional mechanisms (“healed by the elect, by the psalms and prayers and blessings”); this is cosmos→contemporary practice/institution, so the whole paragraph is later pastoral use of the analogy.

paragraphs.core_text: Also, [this] is the other person [who] struck the comrade of the [...] sick with his [...] he struck in [...] he being cruel according to [...] living soul [...] upon it [...] that [...] accusation of [...]
paragraphs.temporal_note: Highly fragmentary continuation that still reads as part of the analogical unit contrasting ‘cruel striking’ with ‘healing cutting’. Mention of “living soul” could be a bridge toward application, but there is still no church/elect/catechumen register here; retained as core with uncertainty due to lacunae.

Seam-flagged institutional extension: catechumens/church language and soteriological bookkeeping (stripping sins, absolution, intercession) that applies the preceding teaching pattern to community practice; per rules this is not MIXED despite possible imitation of teaching syntax.
Institutional summary with catechumen group action and Q&A closure-like movement; dominated by pastoral/church roles and lacks impersonal cosmological exposition.
